transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Hi. Yeah, thanks for seeing me. Um, I came in because I just... I can't stop worrying about everything at once. It's like my brain is running a background script that I can't kill. I'm constantly agonizing over my marriage, whether I'm slipping at work... which, by the way, we just did this massive server migration at my company and I was supposed to lead the backend integration, but I spent three days just staring at the code repository thinking I was going to crash the whole system and get fired. 

And then there's the bills, and all these house projects I keep starting and dropping. Like the guest bathroom. I tore up the tile two months ago, and I went to Lowe's to get the new grout, but I started thinking about whether the color would look outdated in five years, and I stood in the aisle for an hour before I just left empty-handed. My wife has to walk on bare concrete in there now. It's just... I'm constantly terrified I'm basically failing as a husband and a father, you know? I just can't turn the worry off.
Do you find that you worry excessively about a number of different things — like work, family, health, and everyday responsibilities — and that this worry is hard to control most days?

Yeah, exactly. I just can't rein it in at all. Even when I tell myself to just, you know, focus on the code right in front of me, or just try to breathe through a workout... one concern just hooks onto another. Before I know it, I'm twenty steps ahead imagining a bad review turning into losing my job, and my family being worse off because of me. 

Which... speaking of workouts, I actually had to freeze my gym membership recently because I usually drive there, but my car started making this weird rattling noise near the steering column. I took it to the mechanic, and he said it was just a loose heat shield, but I swear it sounds like the transmission. Do you know anything about CVT transmissions? My brother-in-law told me to never buy a car with a CVT, but he's also the kind of guy who insists on changing his own oil and ends up spilling it all over the driveway. He did that last Thanksgiving, actually. Completely ruined my sister's azalea bushes. They had to dig up the whole front bed, and the landscaping company charged them a fortune because of the soil contamination. I told him he should have just used a tarp, but he never listens.
Have you noticed any physical symptoms like restlessness, trouble relaxing, or muscle tension when you're worrying?

Yeah, definitely. I feel wound tight pretty much all day long. It's like my shoulders are just permanently locked up, you know? Like I'm bracing for something to hit me. And sitting still just feels completely impossible. I catch myself pacing around my home office between meetings. Which, honestly, is exhausting because my manager, Dave, loves scheduling these back-to-back standups that aren't even really standups. He just talks for forty-five minutes about agile methodologies. He went to this management retreat in Denver last month and now everything has to be a 'sprint.' I don't think he even knows what a sprint actually entails for the database architecture. 

But anyway, yeah, I can't relax. Even when I go to my chess club on Thursday nights, I'm constantly tapping the pieces on the board or bouncing my leg. The guy I usually play against, Martin, gets so irritated by it. Martin's this retired actuary, very meticulous, always brings his own custom weighted wooden pieces. He bought them in Germany, I think. Or maybe Austria? Somewhere in Europe. They're really beautiful, actually, made of carved walnut and maple, but I just can't stop fidgeting with the captured pawns, and I'm pretty sure he's going to stop playing with me if I keep scratching the varnish.
Have you noticed feeling fatigued or having a lack of energy lately, even if you haven't been physically active?

Fatigued? Um, no, not really. I wouldn't say I lack energy at all. If anything, I'm kind of wired all the time, so I haven't noticed feeling physically drained or sluggish. 

But actually, speaking of energy, I spent like four hours the other night researching solar panels for the house because our electric bill just completely spiked this past quarter. My neighbor, Greg, got them installed last spring, and he went with this company that uses these high-efficiency monocrystalline panels. Which sounded great on paper, but the installation crew completely messed up his roof flashing. Water leaked right into his attic during that massive rainstorm we had back in October. It completely ruined all of his wife's childhood photo albums. She was devastated, obviously. I told him he needed to threaten to sue the contractor, but Greg is just... he's way too passive. He ended up paying out of pocket to hire a guy to fix the drywall. I could never do that. If someone drilled holes in my roof and caused a leak, I'd be on the phone with a lawyer in five minutes. You have to hold people accountable, you know? Especially with contractors, they'll cut corners the second you look away. 

But, um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being tired. No, I haven't really experienced that.
Have you found it hard to concentrate or focus on tasks because your mind is preoccupied with worries?

Yeah, it's really bad actually. Like, during sprint planning or when I'm doing code reviews, I'll read the exact same design note three or four times and I still end up missing details. It's because part of my mind is just completely somewhere else, you know? I'm off calculating what I might have forgot at home, or I'm stressing over how badly the next argument is going to go. 

Which, speaking of forgetting things at home, I actually left my smart lock fob on the kitchen island yesterday. I had to use the backup keypad on the door to get in, but the battery on the keypad has been flashing red for like three weeks. I bought replacement batteries—those weird CR123A ones—but they're sitting in the glovebox of my car. I ordered them in bulk off Amazon, but you have to be so careful with Amazon batteries now because of all the third-party counterfeits. My buddy Mark bought some for his smoke detectors last month, and they died in two days. The smoke detector started chirping at 3 AM. He lives in this old Victorian house over in the historic district, so the ceilings are like twelve feet high, and he had to drag a heavy wooden ladder up from his basement in the middle of the night just to reach the thing. He actually slipped on the bottom step and bruised his tailbone pretty badly. He couldn't sit in his office chair for a month, he had to use one of those inflatable donut pillows. I told him he should have just called the fire department non-emergency line to help him reach it, but Mark is incredibly stubborn. 

But, yeah, anyway, my focus is just completely shot. I just can't keep my mind on the code.

Have you ever experienced sudden episodes of intense fear or discomfort that came on very quickly and included symptoms like a racing heart, shortness of breath, or a feeling like you were losing control?

No, I don't think I've ever had anything like that. Like a panic attack, right? No, I've never had one of those. I mean, my heart races sometimes, but it's not like a sudden explosion of fear or anything. It's more of a constant hum of stress. 

My sister, though, she used to get them all the time when she was in grad school. She was studying architecture at Cornell, and the studio culture there is just completely toxic. They expect you to stay up for three days straight building these intricate balsa wood models. She had this one professor, Professor Vance, who would literally walk around with a metal ruler and smash people's models if he didn't like the structural integrity. Can you imagine? Paying sixty thousand dollars a year in tuition just to have some guy destroy your work with a ruler? She called me crying one night from the studio floor because her hands were shaking so badly she couldn't glue the tiny little window frames on her final project. She ended up having to go to the campus health center, and they gave her some kind of breathing exercises to do. But honestly, I think she just needed to sleep. She was living off of espresso and those weird protein bars that taste like chalk. 

But anyway, no, I've never experienced anything sudden or intense like you're describing. Just the constant worrying.
